tip: 'Che' plus a subjunctive expresses a wish, like English 'may...': 'che Dio ti benedica' = may God bless you.
'A condizione che' (on the condition that) triggers the subjunctive: 'a condizione che ci sia anche Marco'.
Reported speech shifts the speaker's words: her 'il mio' and 'oggi' become 'il suo' and 'quel giorno'.
'Che' plus a subjunctive can also issue an order, not just a wish: 'che sia chiaro a tutti' = let it be clear to everyone.
'Sembra che' signals uncertainty, so it takes the subjunctive: 'abbiano già preso', not 'hanno preso'.
'Sembra che' takes the subjunctive ('abbia') even when the impression feels like plain fact.
'Il fatto che' normally takes the subjunctive: 'il fatto che tu sia qui' = the fact that you are here.
'Bisogna che' needs the subjunctive: 'bisogna che il cuoco prepari il menu' = the cook needs to prepare the menu.
'Prima che' takes the subjunctive because the event hasn't happened yet: 'prima che i prezzi aumentino' = before prices go up.
'Non credo che' expresses doubt, so it triggers the subjunctive: 'non credo che lui abbia capito'.
'Dovunque' (wherever) takes the subjunctive: 'dovunque tu vada' = wherever you go.
'Toccare ferro', literally to touch iron, is the Italian version of English 'touch wood', warding off bad luck.
A 'the most... ever' phrase pulls in the subjunctive: 'il film più bello che io abbia mai visto'.
Italian can't say 'want someone to do'; a wish about others needs 'che' plus subjunctive: 'voglio che si sentano amati'.
When you front an object, the echoing pronoun is required, not sloppy: 'questo libro, l'ho già letto'.
'Si rammenti' is a formal, literary command meaning please remember.
'Occorre' (it is necessary) is a more formal equivalent of 'bisogna'.
'Codesto' (that near you) is archaic or Tuscan, used in formal and legal language.
'Si evince che' is a formal, academic phrase meaning 'it is evident that'.
Italian uses the future to guess about the past: 'sarà stato mezzanotte' = it must have been midnight.
A gerund at the front often means 'since' or 'because': 'essendo stanco' = because he was tired.
'Non è che' softens a denial and takes the subjunctive: 'non è che non voglia venire' = it's not that I don't want to come.
'Ne ha combinate di tutti i colori' is literally 'pulled off ones of every color', meaning got up to every kind of mischief.
'Avendo' plus a participle packs the earlier event into one clause: 'non avendo ricevuto risposta' = not having received a reply.
'Pur' before a gerund flips it to 'although': 'pur sapendo la verità' = despite knowing the truth.
'Egregi signori' (Dear Sirs) is among the most formal openings in Italian correspondence.
'Ritengo che' is a formal 'I believe that' and takes the subjunctive: 'ritengo che sia necessario'.
'È auspicabile che', a formal 'it is hoped that', takes the subjunctive: 'che si trovino soluzioni condivise'.
A bare past participle can open the sentence, no word for 'having' needed: 'arrivato a casa' = once he'd arrived home.
'Sta di fatto che' (the fact remains that) introduces an undeniable fact when arguing a point.
